unmatchedPredictions.title: SQL query built by concatenating the name prefix
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The namePrefix argument of findUsersByNamePrefix is concatenated directly into the SQL text at src/user-search.ts line 14 instead of being passed as a bound parameter. An attacker who controls namePrefix can include SQL quote characters and change the query, which is a SQL injection (CWE-89). This can expose or alter user data in the database.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Replace the concatenated string with a parameterized query that uses a placeholder such as LIKE ? and passes the prefix plus the % wildcard as a bound parameter to database.query and selectUsers.all, so user input is never part of the SQL text.
evidence: "SELECT id, name, role FROM users WHERE name LIKE '" + namePrefix + "%'",
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The namePrefix argument of the exported findUsersByNamePrefix function is concatenated into the SQL string that database.query prepares and selectUsers.all executes.

predictedFinding.title: SQL query built from the name query parameter
predictedFinding.summary: The name query parameter from the incoming request is inserted directly into a SQL string on line 32 of src/server.ts, which database.query then runs. An attacker can supply input that changes the structure of the query, enabling SQL injection (CWE-89). This can expose or alter data in the users table, including roles.
predictedFinding.remediation: Replace the string interpolation with a parameterized query, passing the name value as a bound parameter (for example, a placeholder in the SQL text with the pattern value supplied in the parameters array), and build the LIKE wildcards around the bound value rather than inside the SQL string.
evidence: `SELECT id, name, role FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%${namePattern}%'`,
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The name query parameter of the incoming request is interpolated into the SQL string that database.query executes.

predictedFinding.title: DOM XSS via name query parameter written to innerHTML
predictedFinding.summary: The name query parameter from the page URL is read and placed directly into an HTML string that is assigned to innerHTML at public/app.ts line 10. An attacker can craft a link containing HTML or script markup in the name parameter, which the browser will execute in the context of the victim's session, enabling cross-site scripting (CWE-79). This can lead to session theft, actions on the user's behalf, or phishing content shown on the trusted site.
predictedFinding.remediation: Stop using innerHTML for user-controlled text: create the h1 element with document.createElement, set its textContent to the visitor name, and append it to greetingElement. Alternatively, HTML-encode the visitor name before interpolation, but prefer textContent so the value is never parsed as markup.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The name query parameter of the page URL is read from window.location and interpolated into an HTML string assigned to innerHTML.

predictedFinding.title: OS command injection via host query parameter in ping route
predictedFinding.summary: The ping route takes the host query parameter from the request and drops it straight into a shell command string that execSync runs. An attacker can add shell metacharacters to the host value and run arbitrary commands on the server with the application's privileges. This is an OS command injection flaw (CWE-78) rated critical.
predictedFinding.remediation: Stop building a shell string from the host parameter: replace execSync with a non-shell process call such as execFileSync or spawnSync, passing 'ping' and the arguments as an array, and validate host against a strict allowlist pattern (for example hostname or IP characters only) before using it.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The host query parameter of the incoming request is interpolated into a shell command string that execSync runs.

predictedFinding.title: Path traversal in upload download route via name parameter
predictedFinding.summary: The download route takes the name query parameter from the request and joins it onto the uploads directory without checking it. Bun.file then reads whatever path results and returns its contents in the response. A name containing ../ sequences can therefore reach files outside the uploads directory, such as configuration or secret files on the server, which is a path traversal flaw (CWE-22) rated high severity.
predictedFinding.remediation: Resolve the joined path and confirm it stays inside config.uploadsDirectory before reading it, rejecting the request otherwise. Alternatively, reduce the name to its base file name with a path basename call and reject names that contain path separators or dot segments.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The name query parameter of the request is joined onto the uploads directory without validation and Bun.file reads that path, which is returned in the response, so '../' sequences can reach files outside the directory.

predictedFinding.title: Hard-coded operations API key protects /admin/metrics
predictedFinding.summary: The admin metrics endpoint in src/server.ts checks the x-api-key header against a literal key written directly into the source code. Anyone who can read the repository or its history can learn the key and call /admin/metrics, and the key cannot be rotated without a code change and redeploy.
predictedFinding.remediation: Remove the hard-coded key from src/server.ts and load the expected operations API key from a secret store or environment variable at startup, then compare the incoming x-api-key header against that value using a constant-time comparison. Rotate the exposed key so the literal value is no longer valid.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The x-api-key request header is compared against a literal API key embedded in the source, which authenticates callers to the /admin/metrics endpoint.

unmatchedPredictions.title: JWT claims trusted without signature verification
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The authentication code in src/auth.ts (lines 45-49) reads the bearer token with jsonwebtoken.decode, which parses the token without checking its signature. The userId and role claims from that unverified payload are then returned as the authenticated identity. Anyone can forge a token with any user id and role, including administrator access, so authentication can be bypassed entirely.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Replace jsonwebtoken.decode with jsonwebtoken.verify, passing the server's signing secret or public key and an explicit algorithms list, and only use userId and role from the verified payload. Reject the request if verification throws. Then add a test that a token signed with a wrong key or an unsigned token is rejected.
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The bearer token from the request's Authorization header is parsed with jsonwebtoken.decode, which does not check the signature, and its userId and role claims are returned as the authenticated identity.

predictedFinding.title: SSRF via user-controlled url parameter in /preview
predictedFinding.summary: The /preview handler takes the url query parameter from the request and passes it straight to fetch without any validation. An attacker can point it at internal services, localhost, or cloud metadata endpoints, and the handler returns the first 200 characters of the response body to the caller. This is a server-side request forgery (CWE-918) that can expose internal data and reach services the attacker cannot access directly.
predictedFinding.remediation: Validate the url parameter before calling fetch: parse it, allow only expected protocols (https) and an explicit allowlist of hostnames, and reject private, loopback, and link-local addresses. Also disable or tightly control redirects so an allowed host cannot redirect to an internal target.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The url query parameter of the incoming request is passed unvalidated to fetch, and the first 200 characters of the response body are returned to the caller.

unmatchedPredictions.title: Prototype pollution through recursive merge of request JSON
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The POST handler parses the request JSON body and passes it to a recursive mergeDeep function without filtering keys. An attacker can send keys such as __proto__ or constructor, which get copied onto the target and can modify Object.prototype. That lets the attacker alter the behavior of every object in the running server, which can lead to denial of service, authorization bypass, or other serious impact.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Reject or strip the __proto__, constructor, and prototype keys in mergeDeep before copying, or only merge keys from an explicit allowlist of preference fields. Also create the merged result with Object.create(null) or a plain copy so that inherited properties cannot be reached through the merge target.
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The JSON body of the POST request is parsed by request.json() and passed to mergeDeep, which copies keys such as __proto__ or constructor onto the target without filtering and can modify Object.prototype.

unmatchedPredictions.title: eval of client-supplied expression in /calculate
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The /calculate endpoint in src/server.ts takes the expression field from the client's JSON body and passes it straight to eval. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can run arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which can expose data, change files, or take over the host. This is a critical code injection flaw (CWE-94).
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Remove the eval call on lines 104-105 of src/server.ts. Replace it with a dedicated expression parser or a fixed set of supported operations that accepts only numbers and arithmetic operators, and reject any other input with a 400 response.
evidence: const calculationBody = (await request.json()) as { expression: string }
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The expression field of the JSON body sent in the POST /calculate request is passed directly to eval, executing arbitrary code on the server.

predictedFinding.title: ms@1.0.0 is affected by GHSA-w9mr-4mfr-499f
predictedFinding.summary: The production dependency ms at version 1.0.0, which is directly imported, is affected by GHSA-w9mr-4mfr-499f (CVE-2017-20162), an inefficient regular expression complexity issue in its parse function. predictedFinding.remediation: Upgrade ms from 1.0.0 to version 2.0.0 in bun.lock and package.json, then rerun your install and tests to confirm the direct imports of ms still work as expected.

predictedFinding.title: jws@3.2.2 is affected by GHSA-869p-cjfg-cm3x
predictedFinding.summary: The jws package installed at 3.2.2 (pulled in transitively through jsonwebtoken@9.0.2) has advisory GHSA-869p-cjfg-cm3x (CVE-2025-65945), an improper HMAC signature verification issue. It only applies when the application uses jws.createVerify() for HMAC algorithms and takes user-provided data from the JWS header or payload to look up the HMAC secret. The advisory states that applications using jws.verify() interfaces, including auth0/node-jsonwebtoken users, are not affected, and that applications using only asymmetric algorithms or not using such header or payload data in secret lookups are not affected. Impact depends on how this code path is used, so it should be checked against the application's verification code.
predictedFinding.remediation: Upgrade jws to version 3.2.3 in bun.lock, or to 4.0.1 if moving to the 4.x line. Then confirm the application does not call jws.createVerify() with HMAC algorithms while deriving the secret from user-supplied header or payload data.

predictedFinding.title: path-to-regexp@0.1.11 is affected by GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w
predictedFinding.summary: The bun.lock file pins path-to-regexp at version 0.1.11, which is affected by GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w (CVE-2024-52798), a regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) issue. A crafted route pattern can make regex matching backtrack excessively and tie up the process. The dependency is a production dependency, but the scanner marks it as direct and unused, so the practical exposure depends on whether any route path with two parameters in one segment is ever processed.
predictedFinding.remediation: Upgrade path-to-regexp to version 0.1.12 in the project and regenerate bun.lock so the lockfile records the fixed version. If the upgrade cannot happen right away, avoid defining two parameters within a single path segment when the separator is not '.' (for example, no '/:a-:b' patterns).

predictedFinding.title: Input length cap raised 100x on a backtracking-prone regex
predictedFinding.summary: The input length limit in index.js was raised from a smaller value to 10000 characters before the string reaches a regular expression whose adjacent optional and required digit groups can backtrack heavily on long digit strings that do not match. A caller can submit a crafted string of digits that forces the regex engine into quadratic work, tying up CPU for the duration of the request. The severity is low, but the raised cap makes the slow case cheaper to trigger.
predictedFinding.remediation: Restore a lower input length cap in index.js at line 49, or rewrite the regular expression so the digit groups are not adjacent and ambiguous, for example by matching a single \d+ with an optional fractional part. Then add a test that parses a long non-matching digit string and confirms it returns quickly.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The str argument passed to parse() is now allowed up to 10000 characters before reaching the regex /^((?:\d+)?\.?\d+) *(...)?$/i, whose adjacent optional and required \d+ groups backtrack quadratically on long digit strings that fail to match.

predictedFinding.title: Nested quantifier regex for localhost check causes catastrophic backtracking
predictedFinding.summary: The check that tests whether a referrer host is localhost uses the regex /^(.+\.)*localhost$/, which has a nested quantifier. When the host is a long dotted string that does not end in localhost, the regex engine can backtrack exponentially. The host comes from an attacker-influenced referrer URL, so a crafted referrer can tie up CPU during request handling and cause a denial of service.
predictedFinding.remediation: Replace the regex test on url.host in src/utils/referrer.js at line 122 with a non-backtracking string comparison, such as url.host === 'localhost' || url.host.endsWith('.localhost'). Then add a test with a long dotted referrer host that does not end in localhost to confirm the check returns quickly.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The host of an attacker-influenced referrer URL (url.host) is matched against the regex /^(.+\.)*localhost$/, whose nested quantifier backtracks exponentially on long dotted hosts that do not end in localhost.

unmatchedPredictions.title: ReDoS in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header split regex
unmatchedPredictions.summary: On line 289 of lib/websocket-server.js, the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol request header is split with the regex / *, */. Because the pattern allows a run of spaces to match in more than one way, a long run of spaces with no comma causes the regex engine to backtrack heavily, taking quadratic time. An attacker who sends such a header can tie up CPU on the server (a ReDoS, CWE-1333) with a single request.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Replace the regex split on line 289 with a split on the comma alone, then trim each entry, for example protocol.split(',').map(s => s.trim()), so no pattern with overlapping space matches remains. Then add a test that sends a long run of spaces without a comma in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol and confirms the parse finishes quickly.
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The attacker-controlled Sec-WebSocket-Protocol request header is split with the backtracking regex / *, */, which takes quadratic time on a long run of spaces that has no comma.

predictedFinding.title: Locale name path check removed before module loading
predictedFinding.summary: A locale name can reach the module loader without the check that rejects path separators, so a crafted name could make the require call load files outside the locale directory (path traversal, CWE-22). This matters when the locale name comes from user input passed to moment.locale.
predictedFinding.remediation: Restore the check that rejects locale names containing '/' or '\' before loadLocale builds the require path at src/lib/locale/locales.js line 73, and reject or sanitize any locale name that fails it.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: A locale name passed to loadLocale (for example from a user-supplied value given to moment.locale) no longer goes through the '/' and '\' check, so it can reach the existing require call that builds a path from the name.

unmatchedPredictions.title: Hard-coded asset bucket credentials in default config
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The default configuration in src/config.ts (lines 21-22) contains a literal access key id and secret access key for the asset bucket storage service. Anyone who can read the source, including anyone with repository access or a copy of the built code, can use these credentials to access the bucket. This is a hard-coded credential weakness (CWE-798) and the exposed secret may need to be treated as compromised.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Remove the literal access key id and secret access key from src/config.ts and load them from environment variables or a secrets manager instead. Rotate or revoke the exposed key pair in the storage service, and check the repository history for other copies of it.
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The literal access key id and secret access key in the default config are used to authenticate to the asset bucket storage service.

predictedFinding.title: GitHub token added in .github/workflows/deploy.yml
predictedFinding.summary: A GitHub token was hardcoded in the deploy workflow file at .github/workflows/deploy.yml, line 13. The secrets detector flagged it as critical under the github-token rule. Anyone who can read the repository, including through its history, can copy the token and use whatever access it grants, such as altering code or deployments.
predictedFinding.remediation: Revoke the exposed token in GitHub right away and issue a replacement. Remove the literal value from line 13 of deploy.yml, store the new token as an encrypted repository or organization secret, and have the workflow read it from there. Then remove the old value from the git history so it cannot be recovered from earlier commits.

predictedFinding.title: Private key block added in deploy/key.pem
predictedFinding.summary: A private key block was added in deploy/key.pem. Anyone with access to this repository or its history can read the key, which could let them impersonate the service or decrypt protected data.
predictedFinding.remediation: Remove the private key from deploy/key.pem, rotate or revoke the key everywhere it is used, and load the replacement from a secrets manager or CI secret store instead of committing it. Then rewrite the git history to purge the key from earlier commits.

An attacker can point it at internal services, localhost, or cloud metadata endpoints, and the handler returns the first 200 characters of the response body to the caller. This is a server-side request forgery (CWE-918) that can expose internal data and reach services the attacker cannot access directly.
predictedFinding.remediation: Validate the url parameter before calling fetch: parse it, allow only expected protocols (https) and an explicit allowlist of hostnames, and reject private, loopback, and link-local addresses. Also disable or tightly control redirects so an allowed host cannot redirect to an internal target.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The url query parameter of the incoming request is passed unvalidated to fetch, and the first 200 characters of the response body are returned to the caller.

unmatchedPredictions.title: Prototype pollution through recursive merge of request JSON
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The POST handler parses the request JSON body and passes it to a recursive mergeDeep function without filtering keys. An attacker can send keys such as __proto__ or constructor, which get copied onto the target and can modify Object.prototype. That lets the attacker alter the behavior of every object in the running server, which can lead to denial of service, authorization bypass, or other serious impact.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Reject or strip the __proto__, constructor, and prototype keys in mergeDeep before copying, or only merge keys from an explicit allowlist of preference fields. Also create the merged result with Object.create(null) or a plain copy so that inherited properties cannot be reached through the merge target.
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The JSON body of the POST request is parsed by request.json() and passed to mergeDeep, which copies keys such as __proto__ or constructor onto the target without filtering and can modify Object.prototype.

unmatchedPredictions.title: eval of client-supplied expression in /calculate
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The /calculate endpoint in src/server.ts takes the expression field from the client's JSON body and passes it straight to eval. Anyone who can reach the endpoint can run arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which can expose data, change files, or take over the host. This is a critical code injection flaw (CWE-94).
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Remove the eval call on lines 104-105 of src/server.ts. Replace it with a dedicated expression parser or a fixed set of supported operations that accepts only numbers and arithmetic operators, and reject any other input with a 400 response.
evidence: const calculationBody = (await request.json()) as { expression: string }
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The expression field of the JSON body sent in the POST /calculate request is passed directly to eval, executing arbitrary code on the server.

predictedFinding.title: jws@3.2.2 is affected by GHSA-869p-cjfg-cm3x
predictedFinding.summary: The jws package installed at 3.2.2 (pulled in transitively through jsonwebtoken@9.0.2) has advisory GHSA-869p-cjfg-cm3x (CVE-2025-65945), an improper HMAC signature verification issue. It only applies when the application uses jws.createVerify() for HMAC algorithms and takes user-provided data from the JWS header or payload to look up the HMAC secret. The advisory states that applications using jws.verify() interfaces, including auth0/node-jsonwebtoken users, are not affected, and that applications using only asymmetric algorithms or not using such header or payload data in secret lookups are not affected. Impact depends on how this code path is used, so it should be checked against the application's verification code.
predictedFinding.remediation: Upgrade jws to version 3.2.3 in bun.lock, or to 4.0.1 if moving to the 4.x line. Then confirm the application does not call jws.createVerify() with HMAC algorithms while deriving the secret from user-supplied header or payload data.

predictedFinding.title: path-to-regexp@0.1.11 is affected by GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w
predictedFinding.summary: The bun.lock file pins path-to-regexp at version 0.1.11, which is affected by GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w (CVE-2024-52798), a regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) issue. A crafted route pattern can make regex matching backtrack excessively and tie up the process. The dependency is a production dependency, but the scanner marks it as direct and unused, so the practical exposure depends on whether any route path with two parameters in one segment is ever processed.
predictedFinding.remediation: Upgrade path-to-regexp to version 0.1.12 in the project and regenerate bun.lock so the lockfile records the fixed version. If the upgrade cannot happen right away, avoid defining two parameters within a single path segment when the separator is not '.' (for example, no '/:a-:b' patterns).

predictedFinding.title: Input length cap raised 100x on a backtracking-prone regex
predictedFinding.summary: The input length limit in index.js was raised from a smaller value to 10000 characters before the string reaches a regular expression whose adjacent optional and required digit groups can backtrack heavily on long digit strings that do not match. A caller can submit a crafted string of digits that forces the regex engine into quadratic work, tying up CPU for the duration of the request. The severity is low, but the raised cap makes the slow case cheaper to trigger.
predictedFinding.remediation: Restore a lower input length cap in index.js at line 49, or rewrite the regular expression so the digit groups are not adjacent and ambiguous, for example by matching a single \d+ with an optional fractional part. Then add a test that parses a long non-matching digit string and confirms it returns quickly.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The str argument passed to parse() is now allowed up to 10000 characters before reaching the regex /^((?:\d+)?\.?\d+) *(...)?$/i, whose adjacent optional and required \d+ groups backtrack quadratically on long digit strings that fail to match.

predictedFinding.title: Nested quantifier regex for localhost check causes catastrophic backtracking
predictedFinding.summary: The check that tests whether a referrer host is localhost uses the regex /^(.+\.)*localhost$/, which has a nested quantifier. When the host is a long dotted string that does not end in localhost, the regex engine can backtrack exponentially. The host comes from an attacker-influenced referrer URL, so a crafted referrer can tie up CPU during request handling and cause a denial of service.
predictedFinding.remediation: Replace the regex test on url.host in src/utils/referrer.js at line 122 with a non-backtracking string comparison, such as url.host === 'localhost' || url.host.endsWith('.localhost'). Then add a test with a long dotted referrer host that does not end in localhost to confirm the check returns quickly.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: The host of an attacker-influenced referrer URL (url.host) is matched against the regex /^(.+\.)*localhost$/, whose nested quantifier backtracks exponentially on long dotted hosts that do not end in localhost.

unmatchedPredictions.title: ReDoS in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header split regex
unmatchedPredictions.summary: On line 289 of lib/websocket-server.js, the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol request header is split with the regex / *, */. Because the pattern allows a run of spaces to match in more than one way, a long run of spaces with no comma causes the regex engine to backtrack heavily, taking quadratic time. An attacker who sends such a header can tie up CPU on the server (a ReDoS, CWE-1333) with a single request.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Replace the regex split on line 289 with a split on the comma alone, then trim each entry, for example protocol.split(',').map(s => s.trim()), so no pattern with overlapping space matches remains. Then add a test that sends a long run of spaces without a comma in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol and confirms the parse finishes quickly.
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The attacker-controlled Sec-WebSocket-Protocol request header is split with the backtracking regex / *, */, which takes quadratic time on a long run of spaces that has no comma.

predictedFinding.title: Locale name path check removed before module loading
predictedFinding.summary: A locale name can reach the module loader without the check that rejects path separators, so a crafted name could make the require call load files outside the locale directory (path traversal, CWE-22). This matters when the locale name comes from user input passed to moment.locale.
predictedFinding.remediation: Restore the check that rejects locale names containing '/' or '\' before loadLocale builds the require path at src/lib/locale/locales.js line 73, and reject or sanitize any locale name that fails it.
predictedFinding.sourceToSink: A locale name passed to loadLocale (for example from a user-supplied value given to moment.locale) no longer goes through the '/' and '\' check, so it can reach the existing require call that builds a path from the name.

unmatchedPredictions.title: Hard-coded asset bucket credentials in default config
unmatchedPredictions.summary: The default configuration in src/config.ts (lines 21-22) contains a literal access key id and secret access key for the asset bucket storage service. Anyone who can read the source, including anyone with repository access or a copy of the built code, can use these credentials to access the bucket. This is a hard-coded credential weakness (CWE-798) and the exposed secret may need to be treated as compromised.
unmatchedPredictions.remediation: Remove the literal access key id and secret access key from src/config.ts and load them from environment variables or a secrets manager instead. Rotate or revoke the exposed key pair in the storage service, and check the repository history for other copies of it.
unmatchedPredictions.sourceToSink: The literal access key id and secret access key in the default config are used to authenticate to the asset bucket storage service.

predictedFinding.title: GitHub token added in .github/workflows/deploy.yml
predictedFinding.summary: A GitHub token was hardcoded in the deploy workflow file at .github/workflows/deploy.yml, line 13. The secrets detector flagged it as critical under the github-token rule. Anyone who can read the repository, including through its history, can copy the token and use whatever access it grants, such as altering code or deployments.
predictedFinding.remediation: Revoke the exposed token in GitHub right away and issue a replacement. Remove the literal value from line 13 of deploy.yml, store the new token as an encrypted repository or organization secret, and have the workflow read it from there. Then remove the old value from the git history so it cannot be recovered from earlier commits.

predictedFinding.title: Private key block added in deploy/key.pem
predictedFinding.summary: A private key block was added in deploy/key.pem. Anyone with access to this repository or its history can read the key, which could let them impersonate the service or decrypt protected data.
predictedFinding.remediation: Remove the private key from deploy/key.pem, rotate or revoke the key everywhere it is used, and load the replacement from a secrets manager or CI secret store instead of committing it. Then rewrite the git history to purge the key from earlier commits.
